title: Remove duplicates from a sorted array in-place (slow=insert position, fast=scan).
shortTitle: Remove Duplicates from a Sorted Array In-Place

s1_definition.profdef: Removing duplicates from a sorted array in-place uses two pointers: a slow pointer marking the last position of a unique run, and a fast pointer scanning ahead. Because the array is sorted, duplicates sit next to each other, so whenever the fast pointer finds a value different from the one at the slow pointer, you advance the slow pointer and copy the new value there. The count of unique elements is the slow pointer plus one, achieved in linear time with constant extra space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has a sorted list of the distinct account identifiers that touched a settlement run, but the raw list repeats each identifier once per transaction. The bank wants each identifier only once. A clerk keeps a finger on the last unique identifier written and runs another finger down the list; every time the scanning finger lands on a new identifier different from the last unique one, the clerk writes it just after the kept position. The front of the list ends up holding each identifier exactly once.
s1_definition.oneliner: Slow pointer holds the last unique value; when fast finds a new value, bump slow and copy it there.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Removing duplicates from a sorted array in-place uses two pointers: a slow pointer marking the last position of a unique run, and a fast pointer scanning ahead. Because the array is sorted, duplicates sit next to each other, so whenever the fast pointer finds a value different from the one at the slow pointer, you advance the slow pointer and copy the new value there. The count of unique elements is the slow pointer plus one, achieved in linear time with constant extra space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India has a sorted list of the distinct account identifiers that touched a settlement run, but the raw list repeats each identifier once per transaction. The bank wants each identifier only once. A clerk keeps a finger on the last unique identifier written and runs another finger down the list; every time the scanning finger lands on a new identifier different from the last unique one, the clerk writes it just after the kept position. The front of the list ends up holding each identifier exactly once.

**One line to remember:** Slow pointer holds the last unique value; when fast finds a new value, bump slow and copy it there.

sections.s2_technical:
The precondition is that the array is already sorted, which is what makes this cheap, because equal values are guaranteed to be adjacent, so a single linear scan is enough to collapse runs of duplicates. If the array were not sorted you could not do this in one pass without extra structures.

You start the slow pointer at index zero, treating the first element as already unique. The fast pointer scans from index one to the end. For each fast position, you compare the element there with the element at the slow pointer. If they are equal, it is a duplicate, so you do nothing and let fast move on. If they differ, you have found the next unique value, so you increment slow and copy the fast element into the slow position.

When the scan finishes, the first slow-plus-one positions of the array contain the unique values in order, and the count of uniques is slow plus one. The elements beyond that prefix are leftover and considered logically removed; in Java you typically return the new length and treat the array prefix as the valid data, since Java arrays cannot be resized. If you need an exactly-sized result, you copy the prefix into a new array of that length.

A senior point is that this only removes duplicates; it does not shrink the backing array, because arrays are fixed size. So the honest contract is that the method returns the new logical length, and the caller must respect that length and ignore the tail. Documenting this clearly avoids callers reading stale data in the tail.

Another senior point is comparison correctness. For objects, including BigDecimal, you compare with compareTo or equals appropriately rather than the equality operator, which compares references. For BigDecimal specifically, two values like one point zero and one point zero zero are equal numerically but not by equals because of scale, so if numeric equality is intended I use compareTo equal to zero to detect duplicates, which is a subtle but important choice in finance.

A small finance-domain example: `int slow = 0; for (int fast = 1; fast < ids.length; fast++) { if (ids[fast].compareTo(ids[slow]) != 0) { slow++; ids[slow] = ids[fast]; } } int uniqueCount = slow + 1;` collapses a sorted identifier array to its distinct prefix.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India produces a sorted list of the account identifiers that participated in a settlement run, but because an account can appear in many transactions the list repeats identifiers. A downstream notification service must message each distinct account exactly once, so the pipeline must collapse the sorted list to unique identifiers without allocating a large second list, since the run can be huge. Removing duplicates in place with the slow-fast two pointers is exactly this.

This is exactly how in-place duplicate removal works in Java — the slow pointer keeps the last unique value and the fast pointer copies forward each new distinct value.

Problem 2 — Identifiers are stored as BigDecimal numeric codes, and numerically equal codes with different trailing scale must be treated as the same account. So the duplicate test must use compareTo equal to zero rather than equals, and the method must return the unique count so the caller knows how much of the prefix is valid without reading the stale tail.

What the code will do: a `DedupeService` with `removeDuplicates(BigDecimal[] sortedIds)` using the two-pointer technique and compareTo, returning the unique count. The demo collapses a sorted settlement identifier list and logs the distinct prefix and count.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the demo
java -cp target/classes com.bank.dedupe.DedupeDemo

# Expected: 3 unique accounts [2001, 3001, 4005]
# (2001 and 2001.00 collapse via compareTo; three 3001 collapse to one).
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the sorted identifiers are `2001, 2001.00, 3001, 3001, 3001, 4005`.

Step 1: The array is non-empty, so we proceed. slow starts at index zero, holding `2001`, treated as the first unique.

Step 2: fast is at index one, holding `2001.00`. compareTo between `2001.00` and `2001` returns zero because they are numerically equal despite the scale difference, so this is a duplicate and we skip it. This is why we use compareTo instead of equals.

Step 3: fast is at index two, holding `3001`. compareTo with the slow value `2001` is non-zero, so it is a new unique. We increment slow to one and copy `3001` into position one. The prefix is now `2001, 3001`.

Step 4: fast is at index three, holding `3001`. compareTo with the slow value `3001` is zero, a duplicate, so we skip. fast at index four is also `3001`, again a duplicate, skipped. The three copies of `3001` collapse to one.

Step 5: fast is at index five, holding `4005`. compareTo with the slow value `3001` is non-zero, so it is unique. We increment slow to two and copy `4005` into position two. The prefix is now `2001, 3001, 4005`.

Step 6: The scan ends. slow is two, so the unique count is slow plus one, which is three. The first three positions hold the distinct accounts, and the caller uses only that prefix, ignoring the stale tail. The notification service will message each of the three accounts once.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T16:20:00Z INFO Unique identifiers = 3 out of 6 total
2026-10-26T16:20:00Z INFO Distinct accounts to notify (3): [2001, 3001, 4005]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input (sorted): [2001, 2001.00, 3001, 3001, 3001, 4005]
    │
    ▼
  slow=0 (2001)
    │ fast=1 2001.00 == 2001 (compareTo) → skip
    │ fast=2 3001 ≠ 2001 → slow=1, a[1]=3001
    │ fast=3 3001 == 3001 → skip
    │ fast=4 3001 == 3001 → skip
    │ fast=5 4005 ≠ 3001 → slow=2, a[2]=4005
    ▼
  prefix [2001, 3001, 4005], uniqueCount = slow+1 = 3
    │  (tail positions 3..5 are stale, ignored)
    ▼
  Output: 3 distinct accounts to notify
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Removing duplicates from a sorted array in place uses two pointers. A slow pointer marks the last position of a unique value, and a fast pointer scans ahead. Because the array is sorted, duplicates are adjacent, so whenever the fast pointer lands on a value different from the one at the slow pointer, I advance the slow pointer and copy the new value there. At the end, the unique count is the slow pointer plus one, and it is all done in one linear pass with constant extra space.

The honest contract I always state is that Java arrays cannot shrink, so the method does not truly delete anything; it compacts the distinct values into the front prefix and returns the new logical length, and the caller must use only that prefix and ignore the stale tail. Making that contract explicit stops callers from reading leftover data.

The finance-specific subtlety is the equality test. For BigDecimal, equals also considers scale, so one thousand and one thousand point zero zero are not equal by equals even though they are numerically the same. When I mean numeric equality I test compareTo equal to zero, which correctly collapses the same account written with different scale.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to collapse a sorted list of account identifiers from a settlement run so the notification service messages each distinct account exactly once, without allocating a huge second list on a large run. Identifiers are numeric BigDecimal codes, so I dedupe by compareTo to treat scale-different values as the same account, and I return the unique count so the caller knows how much of the prefix is valid. Explaining the two-pointer mechanics, the return-length contract, and the compareTo subtlety shows the interviewer that I understand in-place algorithms and the real data-type pitfalls in finance.
